did_you_know.text: Ezekiel is commanded to present the house of Israel with both a riddle and a parable, conveying a prophetic message through images and symbols.
The parable begins with a great eagle, with broad wings and many feathers, coming to Lebanon and taking the top of a cedar.
After taking the top of the cedar, the eagle also takes a seed from the land and plants it in fertile soil beside abundant waters.
The seed becomes a low-growing vine whose roots remain in place as it sends out branches and bears fruit; its low height emphasizes its subordinate position.
The vine turns its roots and branches toward another great eagle and seeks water from it instead of relying on the place where it was first planted.
Beginning with this verse, the prophet is commanded to explain the meaning of the parable to the house of Israel rather than leaving it as a riddle alone.
The interpretation identifies the first eagle with the king of Babylon, who took the king of Jerusalem and his officials and brought them to Babylon.
The king of Babylon took a member of the royal family, made a covenant with him, and bound him by an oath, so that Judah would remain a humble kingdom and not exalt itself.
The rebellion is described as an attempt to turn to Egypt for horses and a large army; yet the prophet asks whether one who breaks a covenant can escape.

The prophecy concludes with an image of hope: the Lord will take a tender sprig from the cedar and plant it on a high mountain in Israel, where it will grow into a mighty cedar that provides shelter for the birds.
